title: Managed disorder: The hard road to a modest peace with Russia after Ukraine - European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Jeremy Shapiro argues the Ukraine war will end in a ceasefire that leaves Russia, Europe and America in open-ended low-grade confrontation, and proposes 'managed disorder' — a five-stage framework of verification, certification and reversible incentives running over 10+ years, governed by an Iran-deal-style qualified-majority mechanism that requires consensus to waive penalties rather than to impose them, so that a single pro-Russian member state cannot quietly block enforcement.

insights.claim: Shapiro opens with a 2028 scenario in which Russian armour moves toward a ceasefire line, shooting starts within 48 hours, and the security guarantors reach for the ceasefire documents only to find they say different things depending on who is reading them.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Textual ambiguity in ceasefire documents is the specific mechanism through which a frozen conflict reignites — the drafting detail investors and analysts should read closely.
insights.quote: The security guarantors reach for the ceasefire documents and find they say different things depending on who is reading them.
insights.locator: After the ceasefire

insights.claim: In the scenario, America is focused since 2027 on a series of interventions in Latin America and nobody has agreed what the rules are, what triggers intervention, what constitutes a proportionate response or who decides.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: US attention diversion to the Western Hemisphere is treated as a live near-term assumption, not a tail risk — an input to any European defence-spending thesis.
insights.locator: Nobody knows what to do

insights.claim: Chaos and escalation driven by uncertainty and domestic political pressure are the conditions that precede catastrophic wars, so the purpose of the framework is to ensure clear answers exist before the shooting starts.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Pre-agreed decision rules are the deliverable that matters; announcements of intent are not a substitute.
insights.locator: The outcome of this scenario is chaos

insights.claim: Adapting Michael Howard's insight, the end of fighting does not itself create peace: between war and peace lies a large and dangerous space of armistices, frozen conflicts and unstable political settlements.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: The mental model for pricing the post-ceasefire period: neither war nor peace, with a persistent probability of reversion.
insights.quote: Between war and peace lies a large and dangerous space of armistices, frozen conflicts and unstable political settlements.
insights.locator: This is not an unusual situation after inconclusive wars

insights.claim: The post-war environment in Europe will be unstable in the near term and perhaps for a generation or more, because the wounds are too deep and the sides too evenly matched to agree a comprehensive peace resolving sovereignty, security, power or identity.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: A generational instability baseline argues for structurally elevated European defence spending regardless of ceasefire headlines.
insights.locator: The goal of this paper is to help prevent that scenario

insights.claim: The ceasefire will probably fail to clarify what counts as a violation, who monitors and enforces it, or who decides when one side has broken it — meaning every troop movement, artillery exchange, drone incident, act of sabotage and political crisis in Kyiv or Moscow becomes a potential escalation trigger.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Post-ceasefire headline risk stays high with no reduction in tail probability — volatility does not fall just because major combat stops.
insights.quote: This is the central danger of the post-war moment.
insights.locator: This state of affairs will be the first source of disorder

insights.claim: For the US, Russia will remain a nuclear power and disruptive actor but no longer the organising threat of American strategy, as Washington increasingly focuses on China, the Western Hemisphere and the fiscal costs of global leadership — while Europe will have no such luxury.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: The transatlantic priority gap is structural, not administration-specific — European defence autonomy spending is a secular rather than cyclical theme.
insights.locator: The second source of disorder lie within the West itself

insights.claim: Europe will fear both American abandonment and American freelancing, needing Washington to work toward managed disorder while no longer being able to count on it to take the lead.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: The two failure modes are opposite in direction, which is why Europe's hedging looks incoherent — a durable source of transatlantic friction.
insights.quote: Europe will fear both American abandonment and American freelancing.
insights.locator: This divergence means that the Atlantic alliance

insights.claim: The war produced a rhetorical European consensus — Ukraine must survive and Europe must do more for its own defence — that hides deep disagreements, with Poland, Sweden and other eastern and northern states judging arrangements through deterrence and Russian deception while Spain, Italy and others weight stability, fiscal pressures and eventual economic normalisation with Russia.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Southern European appetite for economic normalisation with Russia is the specific fault line that sanctions durability will test.
insights.locator: Europe will also generate disorder of its own

insights.claim: Poland will worry that Ukraine's accession — its agricultural exports, corruption and security needs — could transform the EU in ways it cannot control, even while Baltic states want to accelerate Ukraine's integration into the EU and the European defence economy.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Ukrainian agricultural export access is the concrete commercial flashpoint inside the pro-Ukraine camp itself.
insights.locator: Yet others, like Poland, will worry

insights.claim: Russia will create the most obvious disorder but not necessarily through renewed invasion: it may accept a ceasefire believing time is on its side, use the pause to rebuild forces, probe resolve, influence European politics and normalise its gains while formally conceding nothing — so a ceasefire may mark not the end of Russian revisionism but its movement into a different register.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: The base case is hybrid continuation, not renewed conventional war — the risk to price is infrastructure sabotage and political interference, not tanks.
insights.quote: A ceasefire may therefore mark not the end of Russian revisionism, but its movement into a different register.
insights.locator: Russia will create the most obvious source of disorder

insights.claim: Policymakers should not assume Russia fears disorder the way they do: ambiguity helps Moscow test thresholds, hybrid operations impose costs while preserving deniability, and political interference weakens European unity without triggering a military response — making curbing Russia's appetite for turbulence harder than deterring a second invasion.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Deterrence spending on conventional forces addresses the easier problem; the binding gap is grey-zone attribution and response.
insights.quote: For America and Europe, deterring a second invasion of Ukraine may well be the easier task; the harder one will be to curb Russia’s appetite for exploiting turbulence around Europe’s borders.
insights.locator: American and European policymakers should not assume

insights.claim: Spillover will extend beyond Ukraine to Moldova, the Black Sea and the Arctic, while Africa and the Middle East may offer Russia opportunities to punish Europe indirectly through migration, mercenary activity, energy disruption or political leverage.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Names five distinct geographies where Russian coercion can hit European energy, shipping and migration — a checklist of secondary exposure.
insights.locator: The post-war order will also face regional spillover

insights.claim: The final source of disorder is the absence of accepted leaders: the EU cannot speak with the speed or unity of a state, NATO can deter but cannot resolve political disputes a bad ceasefire creates, and in that vacuum private envoys, Gulf intermediaries, business figures, transactional American negotiators and ad hoc coalitions will move in — 'without rules, the system will fill with middlemen'.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Expect commercially motivated private intermediaries to shape post-war arrangements — a governance risk with direct implications for reconstruction contracting.
insights.quote: Without rules, the system will fill with middlemen.
insights.locator: The final source of disorder will come from the absence

insights.claim: Managed disorder requires Ukraine to want to comply rather than be forced to, which means the system must offer tangible, domestically defensible benefits — sustained military aid, joint defence production, reconstruction funding, an EU path and a credible route to recovering lost territory without renewed fighting.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Ukrainian consent is purchased with reconstruction and defence-industrial commitments — the spending is the mechanism, not charity.
insights.quote: Ukraine will not abide by the rules of managed disorder if it experiences it only as a restraint on its actions rather than as a route to a stronger Ukrainian state.
insights.locator: Ukraine is the hinge

insights.claim: Europe should tie the pace of Ukraine's accession — market access, regulatory alignment, reconstruction funding — to Ukraine's conduct within the system, because cooperation opens the door and obstruction closes it, and no Ukrainian government can afford to turn its back on a European future.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: EU accession becomes the primary lever of Western influence over Kyiv's post-war military posture.
insights.locator: The main part of that route goes through EU membership

insights.claim: EU membership's mutual-assistance clause Article 42.7 carries none of NATO's integrated command structure or binding defence commitments, yet Ukrainian officials under domestic pressure may present accession as delivering that protection anyway — leaving the public expecting a NATO-style response the clause was never built to provide.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: A specific expectations mismatch that could produce a credibility crisis; any real guarantee needs its own instrument with defined triggers and decision process.
insights.quote: the bloc’s mutual-assistance clause, Article 42.7, carries none of NATO’s integrated command structure or binding defence commitments
insights.locator: That pull is real, but it has limits

insights.claim: Ukraine will benefit more from sustained military aid, joint defence production and a homegrown arms industry than from any ambiguous or unenforceable security guarantee, needing artillery, air defence, drones and the factories to build them for decades to come.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: A decades-long Ukrainian defence-industrial buildout is the durable investable consequence of the war, more so than any guarantee text.
insights.quote: The country will need artillery, air defence, drones and the factories to build them for decades to come.
insights.locator: In any case, Ukraine will benefit more

insights.claim: Offensive or long-range systems capable of striking deep into Russian territory should come from Western allies only if Russia attacks again, but Ukraine's own expanding arms industry will blur that line because Washington and European capitals can condition transfers yet cannot control what Ukraine builds.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Indigenous Ukrainian long-range production is a structural escalation risk no Western export control can manage.
insights.locator: But offensive or long-range systems

insights.claim: The honest position is that Ukraine cannot retake its territory by force and restoration will come through resilience, European integration, legal non-recognition, diplomacy and long-term shifts in the balance of power — not a bet on a better war later, with West Germany's eventual absorption of the East as the precedent.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Frames occupied-territory recovery as a multi-decade political process, removing military reconquest from any realistic base case.
insights.quote: Ukraine can keep hoping for its territory back without believing that another war is the way to get it.
insights.locator: The territorial question needs careful handling

insights.claim: Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia — Ukraine's strongest backers — must be inside any difficult trade-off, because if they support a compromise Ukrainian leaders can sell it as strengthening Ukraine, while if they oppose it critics will portray the arrangement as a deal made over Ukraine's head.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Frontline-state endorsement is the legitimacy currency for any settlement — watch Warsaw and the Baltics as the political gatekeepers.
insights.locator: Coalition dynamics will shape compliance

insights.claim: The steel porcupine model — a defensible, resilient Ukraine armed to deter but not configured for offensive operations, following cold war West Germany's logic — is the workable middle between a neutralised Ukraine unacceptable to Kyiv and an offensively capable or Western-troop-hosting Ukraine unacceptable to Moscow.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Defines the procurement mix the West should expect to fund: defensive systems, fortification and production capacity, not deep-strike platforms.
insights.quote: This “steel porcupine“ posture follows the same logic as cold war West Germany: strong enough to make conquest costly but not positioned as a launchpad for offensive war.
insights.locator: The path to managed disorder

insights.claim: The paper does not assume Moscow wants peace or even managed disorder; the only assumption is that a ceasefire would reveal some Russian interest in pausing large-scale war, and the task is to exploit that pause to make restraint more attractive than returning to war.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: A deliberately minimal assumption set, which makes the framework robust to Russian bad faith — the analytic discipline to demand of any peace plan.
insights.locator: Russia’s calculations

insights.claim: The logic is structured choice: if Russia complies the rewards should be tangible with sanctions relief immediate but reversible, and if Russia violates the rules suspended sanctions snap back automatically.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Automatic, reversible sanctions relief is the core commercial mechanism — companies re-entering Russia would face permanent contingent exit risk.
insights.locator: The logic is structured choice

insights.claim: Russian weakness should not lull the West into assuming diminished appetite for aggression: Russia's calculation changes only if Ukraine, armed by Europe, can defend itself, so a second invasion would confront a better-prepared Ukraine, a more fortified eastern flank and a Western sanctions system built to escalate rather than merely restore previous penalties.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: The escalation-capable sanctions design is a notable shift from restore-prior-penalties — a higher ceiling on future Russian economic risk.
insights.locator: Military realities can reinforce this logic

insights.claim: The Kremlin has shown it will sacrifice prosperity for war and ideology, but Russians value market access, targeted relief and the ability to travel, so sanctions can create constituencies for restraint if relief is selective, staged, reversible and designed to hurt the specific people and networks benefiting from compliance when escalation resumes.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Targeted, individual-level relief as a political engineering tool — implies granular rather than sectoral sanctions design going forward.
insights.quote: Sanctions can thus create constituencies for restraint.
insights.locator: Economic incentives can also matter

insights.claim: Moscow does not need to like managed disorder to live with it: it only needs to face a world in which restraint brings some gains and cheating brings higher costs, since all any arrangement can do is make every alternative worse.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Removes trust and intent from the design problem entirely — the framework's chief claim to feasibility.
insights.quote: Moscow does not need to like managed disorder to live with it.
insights.locator: Moscow does not need to like managed disorder

themes.theme: Turkey and China as structural constraints

insights.claim: Turkey belongs in the system because Ankara controls Black Sea access through the Bosphorus and Dardanelles, has direct maritime interests and has kept working channels with both Russia and Ukraine — so any arrangement touching naval access, grain routes, energy transport, Russian warship movements or southern coastal security requires Turkish participation.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Turkey holds a structural veto over Black Sea grain and energy logistics — a chokepoint exposure for agricultural and shipping markets.
insights.locator: Turkey as a partner

insights.claim: Ukraine's security depends on Odesa, the country's principal port and the conduit for the bulk of its grain exports, without which Ukraine would be cut off from global maritime trade.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: A single-port dependency is the clearest physical vulnerability in Ukraine's post-war economy and in global grain supply.
insights.locator: The Black Sea requires special attention

insights.claim: China need not endorse managed disorder for its interests to reinforce it: Beijing benefits from a stable Russia that checks Western power but not from a Russia that collapses or continually destabilises Europe, since endless war raises energy prices, invites secondary sanctions and risks escalation disrupting Chinese growth.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Chinese interest in predictability is an underweighted stabilising force — and a channel through which Europe can exert leverage on Moscow.
insights.locator: China in the background

insights.claim: Managed disorder needs a China clause: if Russia uses China to rearm and restock munitions, Europe should tighten its China policy, deepen coordination with America and target Chinese firms enabling violations with economic pressure.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Explicit secondary-sanctions exposure for named Chinese firms is a concrete future risk for China-Europe trade relationships.
insights.quote: Managed disorder also needs a China clause.
insights.locator: Managed disorder also needs a China clause

insights.claim: Western leaders should make clear that stability unlocks better China-Europe economic ties while a collapse of managed disorder would push Europe toward militarisation, protectionism and tighter technological coordination with the United States.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Frames European trade and tech-control policy as an explicit bargaining chip against Chinese support for Russian rearmament.
insights.locator: Economic interests pull in the same direction

insights.claim: Managed disorder rests on three principles: separate where necessary through stronger European defences and less dependence on Russian energy, compartmentalise where possible on nuclear risk, Arctic exploitation, climate and counter-proliferation, and make engagement conditional on specific verifiable benchmarks with reversible rewards.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Reduced Russian energy dependence is treated as a precondition for dialogue, not a byproduct — sustaining the European energy-transition and LNG import build-out.
insights.quote: Effective deterrence is a precondition for any dialogue.
insights.locator: A framework for managed disorder

insights.claim: Stage 1 covering roughly years 0-2 sets baseline rules including no renewed large-scale offensive action, no forcible changes to a clearly delineated line of control, no systematic attacks on European critical infrastructure, no escalatory hybrid campaign against EU or NATO states, and restrictions on long-range missiles near the line of contact.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Explicitly places European infrastructure attacks and hybrid campaigns inside the ceasefire perimeter — expanding what counts as a violation beyond the front line.
insights.locator: Stage 1: Freeze the status quo

insights.claim: Stage 1 should set up a dedicated arbitration channel for property claims, compensation and an inventory of assets in occupied territories, because unresolved property claims — Ukrainian homes and businesses, frozen Russian state and linked private assets across Europe, and European pre-war investment claims — only get harder to settle and easier for spoilers to exploit the longer they sit.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Frozen Russian assets and European pre-war claims will be litigated through a dedicated channel — directly relevant to holders of impaired Russia-linked exposures.
insights.quote: Left unaddressed, these grievances will curdle into domestic pressure against any government trying to sustain the framework.
insights.locator: Property claims will likely be one of the war’s most politically corrosive legacies

insights.claim: Stage 2 covering roughly years 2-4 creates two parallel negotiation tracks — Track A on the Ukraine-Russia contact line and Track B on NATO-Russia military transparency — with progress or failure in one having no bearing on the other and Track B explicitly excluding Ukraine's sovereign choices.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Deliberate track separation is designed to stop Moscow trading Ukrainian concessions for NATO constraints — the key procedural defence for Kyiv.
insights.locator: Two tracks

insights.claim: Stage 2 should create four separate crisis channels: Ukraine-Russia for contact line incidents, NATO-Russia military for exercises and deployments, a political channel bringing together the European core group, US, Ukraine and Russia for sanctions-snapback or escalation cases, and a Black Sea channel with Turkey centrally involved — linked by notification rules but never merged.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Compartmentalisation means a Black Sea shipping incident should not collapse the whole framework — a design feature that reduces correlated escalation risk.
insights.quote: Their value lies precisely in compartmentalisation: failure in one channel should not bring down the rest.
insights.locator: Crisis channels

insights.claim: Stage 3 covering roughly years 4-7 deliberately allows rearmament by Europe, Ukraine and Russia rather than capping it — because caps would be unpopular, hard to verify and damaging to deterrence — while regulating placement, notification, observers, long-range systems and external assistance so that rearmament is less surprising, less offensive in posture and less crisis-prone.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Explicitly no arms-control cap on European or Ukrainian rearmament — the defence-spending upcycle is assumed to run through the whole framework.
insights.quote: In short, managed disorder should allow rearmament but make it less surprising, less offensive in posture and less likely to spark a crisis.
insights.locator: Stage 3: Manage deterrence

insights.claim: Hybrid activity cannot be managed through traditional arms control, but Russia cannot stop the drone war in Ukraine while continuing an infrastructure war across Europe and still expect sanctions relief — so a reduction in major hybrid attacks should become part of the price of entry, enforced through a certification process linking assessed activity to sanctions and diplomatic access.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Sabotage of European infrastructure would carry explicit sanctions consequences — raising the compliance stakes for European utilities and undersea cable operators.
insights.quote: Attribution will remain contested, but the absence of perfect attribution cannot excuse permanent grey-zone coercion.
insights.locator: Hybrid activity is a harder problem

insights.claim: Stage 4 cooperation silos should start soon after a ceasefire in fertiliser and food exports, prisoner exchanges, Black Sea commercial shipping and nuclear safety, then extend into maritime and Arctic search-and-rescue and deconfliction plus space debris monitoring, counter-proliferation and climate data exchange — all governed by a spoiler clause under which major destabilisation in one domain cuts benefits in others.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Fertiliser and food export facilitation is the earliest and most tradeable Russian concession — watch it as the first observable sign the framework is functioning.
insights.locator: Stage 4: Build cooperation silos

insights.claim: The Arctic was one of the few spaces where Russia, America and Europe cooperated despite wider tensions, but that cooperation has collapsed under Finland and Sweden's NATO accession, Russian militarisation of the High North, competition over energy and shipping routes, and Chinese interest in Arctic access.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: The Arctic is now a rivalry theatre with energy and shipping-route stakes and no functioning deconfliction — an underpriced incident risk.
insights.locator: The Arctic presents a distinct challenge

insights.claim: Stage 5 institutionalisation would take more than ten years and may never arrive, with the CSCE launched in the early 1970s only becoming the standing OSCE in 1995 as the benchmark — potential forms include a US-Europe-Russia Risk Reduction Commission and a modular arms-control instrument replacing parts of the CFE and INF frameworks, eventually bringing in China.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: A 25-year institutionalisation horizon sets realistic expectations: no near-term European security treaty architecture is coming.
insights.locator: Stage 5: Institutionalise managed disorder

insights.claim: The framework's incremental logic is that ceasefire enables monitoring, monitoring enables transparency, transparency enables limits, limits enable rules, and rules enable institutions — with each step earned through behaviour rather than granted on faith.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: The single clearest statement of the sequencing dependency — skipping a step is what causes frameworks like this to fail.
insights.quote: The logic is incremental: ceasefire enables monitoring, monitoring enables transparency, transparency enables limits, limits enable rules, rules enable institutions.
insights.locator: The path to stability runs through this framework

themes.theme: Governance to defeat European veto paralysis

insights.claim: Europe needs a core group of countries able to pre-negotiate sanctions positions, military support thresholds, monitoring standards and responses to Russian violations before each crisis arrives — including France, Germany, Poland and the UK plus the Nordic and Baltic states — with the core group driving security logic and EU institutions anchoring the economic, sanctions, enlargement and legitimacy logic.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Names the specific coalition that would actually set European Russia policy — a de facto directorate operating outside the EU27.
insights.locator: That means creating a European core group

insights.claim: The governance model should borrow from the 2015 Iran nuclear deal: participants define upfront what counts as a violation and a compliance milestone, criteria cannot be revised downward, and a standing committee decides by qualified majority whether Russia met a criterion — with the agreed reward or penalty following automatically unless a majority votes to block it.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Flipping the default from consensus-to-act to consensus-to-waive is the mechanism that would make EU sanctions genuinely automatic and durable.
insights.quote: This process flips the usual logic. The current system requires consensus to impose a snapback or advance a tranche of sanctions relief; the new one will require consensus to waive either.
insights.locator: How to overcome division paralysis in Europe

insights.claim: Under this design a hypothetical pro-Russian Hungarian or Slovak government seeking to delay consequences would have to openly vote to do so and bear public responsibility rather than blocking quietly through procedural abstention, while a frontline state like Poland or a Baltic country would need a majority to block rewards once Russia demonstrably meets a milestone.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Converts quiet obstruction into a visible political act — the specific fix for the Hungary problem in EU Russia policy.
insights.locator: This process flips the usual logic

insights.claim: A three-tier proportionality system keeps both cautious and hawkish states invested: minor procedural breaches suspend talks or freeze a tranche of sanctions relief, material violations such as denial of inspection access trigger limited snapback, and major ones such as attacks on defence production trigger full enforcement.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Graduated, pre-defined snapback tiers give sanctions relief a knowable risk profile that businesses could actually underwrite.
insights.locator: A three-tier system would make this balance work

insights.claim: The framework should adopt a presumption-of-violation approach placing the burden on Russia to prove compliance — for example if Russia denies inspectors access to a missile site, the refusal itself counts as a breach and triggers penalties.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Reverses the evidentiary burden that has historically let Russia stall enforcement — the operational core of the design.
insights.quote: The framework must treat future violations as probable and place the burden on Russia to prove it is complying, not on America or Europe to show that it is not.
insights.locator: Operating rules

insights.claim: Russia has consistently used the indivisible security clause of the 1999 Charter for European Security to assert a right to deny its neighbours membership in Western security organisations such as NATO, which is why frontline states fear that discussing basing, exercises or notification requirements at all gives Moscow a path back to influence over their security.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: A documented precedent for how Russia weaponises negotiated language — the reason any regional security talks must be tightly scoped in advance.
insights.locator: This regional security agenda will make many European leaders uncomfortable

insights.claim: European leaders should define in advance the principles governing any regional security conversation — no recognition of territorial conquest, no Russian veto over neighbours' alliance decisions, no limits on Ukraine's sovereign choices and no economic relief without behavioural restraint — because they cannot prevent every American side channel with Moscow but can limit the damage.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Four explicit European red lines that would constrain any US-Russia bilateral deal — the test to apply to whatever Washington negotiates.
insights.locator: Russia will prefer to discuss regional security with America

insights.claim: Bilateral European re-engagement with Russia should be registered, reported to the core group where security-relevant and subject to spoiler clauses, because left unmanaged bilateral contacts could become the pathway through which sanctions erode and Europe fragments.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Identifies uncoordinated national commercial re-engagement as the likeliest mechanism of sanctions erosion — the specific channel to monitor.
insights.quote: Left unmanaged, bilateral contacts could become the pathway through which sanctions erode and Europe fragments.
insights.locator: The task for the bilateral re-engagement

themes.theme: Why the four alternatives are worse

insights.claim: Regime change in Moscow offers no credible path from the present to a better order, because neither the US nor Europe can engineer a liberal transition or rely on sanctions, battlefield losses or elite discontent to produce a palatable successor — a post-Putin Russia could become more nationalist, more chaotic or more determined to prove the war was not lost.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Rules out the succession-optimism trade — betting on a benign post-Putin Russia has no analytic support here.
insights.locator: The first alternative is regime change in Moscow

insights.claim: Permanent isolation will not manage the next phase because sanctions erode without a political strategy, European governments will divide over costs and enforcement, and China, Turkey, the Gulf states and others will create channels around Western pressure while Russia adapts and waits for fatigue.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Sanctions decay is treated as structurally inevitable absent an active political framework — a bearish view on the durability of the current regime.
insights.quote: Sanctions will erode without a political strategy.
insights.locator: The second alternative is permanent isolation

insights.claim: Normalisation without conditions would reward aggression without securing restraint, telling Russia that conquest brings only a temporary crisis followed by eventual reintegration, and engagement has value only as part of a structure of leverage — otherwise it becomes 'appeasement by exhaustion'.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: The argument European businesses pushing for quick re-entry will have to overcome; expect political resistance to unconditional normalisation.
insights.quote: Without that structure, it becomes appeasement by exhaustion.
insights.locator: The third alternative is normalisation

insights.claim: Unmanaged confrontation is the most likely default outcome because it requires no decision — uneven arming of Ukraine, haphazard sanctions, episodic talks, NATO debating deployments only after Russia tests them, and Washington cutting its own deals — producing recurrent improvisation under pressure rather than principled firmness.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: The base case absent deliberate action is drift, which means persistent geopolitical risk premia rather than a post-ceasefire relief rally.
insights.quote: This outcome is the most likely default because it requires no decision.
insights.locator: The fourth alternative is unmanaged confrontation

insights.claim: All four alternatives share a deeper flaw of assuming one element can solve the whole problem — Russian transformation, isolation, reintegration or Western toughness — whereas the post-war confrontation requires deterrence and dialogue, punishment and incentives, European unity and coalitions of the willing, Ukrainian agency, American involvement and European hedging simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: A useful screen for evaluating any Russia policy proposal: single-lever plans collapse when reality supplies the other side of the tension.
insights.quote: Any strategy that chooses only one side of these tensions will collapse when reality supplies the other.
insights.locator: These alternatives also share a deeper flaw

insights.claim: Managed disorder is explicitly not permanent peace, reconciliation or a just settlement but 'an operating system for a bad peace', and the paper concedes it will make no one happy — delivering neither justice for Ukraine, reconciliation with Russia, strategic autonomy for Europe nor a restored US-European consensus.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: Sets the realistic ceiling on post-war outcomes — no scenario in this framework produces a clean geopolitical de-risking event.
insights.quote: It is an operating system for a bad peace.
insights.locator: An operating system for a bad peace

insights.claim: The paper is the product of a working group meeting over more than a year including Samuel Charap of RAND, Ivan Krastev, Hanna Notte, Hiski Haukkala, Bob Deen and Jim O'Brien, and all working group members except Michael Kimmage of the Kennan Institute fully endorse it.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Shapiro
insights.so_what: An explicitly recorded dissent within a heavyweight transatlantic working group signals where elite consensus on Russia policy is not yet settled.
insights.locator: Acknowledgments
